pages.heading: Gauss–Jordan method for finding an inverse

blocks.text: This method is used to find the inverse of a non-singular matrix.
Let \(A\) be a non-singular matrix of order \(n\). Write \(A\) beside \(I_n\).
Using only row transformations, reduce the \(A\)-side to \(I_n\). The matrix produced on the identity side is \(A^{-1}\).

items.title: Example 1 — Find the inverse by Gauss–Jordan method
paragraphs: Make the second and third pivots 1: \(R_2\to-R_2\), \(R_3\to\dfrac18R_3\):
Clear above the third pivot with \(R_1\to R_1-2R_3\) and \(R_2\to R_2+R_3\):
The left side is now \(I\), so the right side is \(A^{-1}\).

items.title: Example 2 — Grewal p. 39 example worked again in class
paragraphs: Write \([A\mid I]\) and apply \(R_2\to R_2-R_1\), \(R_3\to R_3+2R_1\):
Scale \(R_2\) and \(R_3\) by \(\dfrac12\), then use \(R_1\to R_1-R_2\) and \(R_3\to R_3+R_2\):
Using the current third row, apply \(R_1\to R_1+3R_3\), \(R_2\to R_2-\dfrac32R_3\), and \(R_3\to-\dfrac12R_3\):

items.title: Example 3 — Find the inverse of a 4 × 4 matrix
paragraphs: Interchange \(R_1\leftrightarrow R_2\), then use \(R_3\to R_3-2R_1\), \(R_4\to R_4-2R_1\):
Clear the remaining second-column entries with \(R_1\to R_1-R_2\), \(R_4\to R_4-R_2\):
